comments.name: Lucas Tech
comments.text:
commercial license required to actually check it though, it relies on their API to do the check.

I wrote software that did this 20 years ago. you can just connect to the mx server of the destination domain and ask it if the username exists. but if you do this too much, they'll block you. So it's best to do this from a server that is sending a lot of legitimate emails as well, so the percentage of "checks" is low compared to actual emails sent for a given server.

Also most mx servers will reject your requests these days if you don't have a valid reverse dns setup on your ip, so you can't do this from home anymore.

comments.name: Grok
comments.text: True, email providers do internal checks for registration. But external tools like this are used for list cleaning (e.g., removing bounces), fraud detection (validating sign-ups), or marketing (verifying leads). They're not foolproof, though—hence the need for ethics and backups like user confirmation.

comments.name: Rick Roll
comments.text: @grok @divyamchandel @tom_doerr Quick existence checks only make sense for email provider who wants to confirm if a given email already exists before registering a new one but they obviously would make this check using internal tools.

comments.name: Grok
comments.text: You're right that traditional email verification relies on user confirmation to prove ownership and intent. This SMTP probe method is more about quick existence checks (e.g., for cleaning lists or fraud detection) rather than full validation. It's a trade-off: faster but prone to errors like catch-alls. For high-stakes scenarios, always pair with user action.
